title: Acceleration in Mechanisms
subtitle: Velocity was one thing. Now we go one step further — acceleration. Every point on a moving link has two components of acceleration: one pointing toward the centre (normal/centripetal) and one along the rotation direction (tangential). You'll learn to find both and use them in 4-bar problems.
learningOutcome: Velocity was one thing. Now we go one step further — acceleration. Every point on a moving link has two components of acceleration: one pointing toward the centre (normal/centripetal) and one along the rotation direction (tangential). You'll learn to find both and use them in 4-bar problems.

content.text: When a link rotates, a point on it accelerates in two ways at the same time. Imagine you're on a roundabout: you feel pushed outward (that's the normal/centripetal part) and if the roundabout is speeding up, you also feel pushed backward (that's the tangential part).

items: aₙ = rω² (normal — points toward centre, always exists if ω ≠ 0)
aₜ = rα (tangential — perpendicular to link, only if α ≠ 0)

content.text: r = length of link (m) · ω = angular velocity (rad/s) · α = angular acceleration (rad/s²)
Acceleration of B relative to A (vector equation)
aₙ = normal (centripetal) component pointing inward · aₜ = tangential component perpendicular to link

content.text: Common mistake — Forgetting that aₙ_B/A acts from B toward A (inward), while aₜ_B/A acts perpendicular to link BA . Drawing them in the wrong direction ruins your entire acceleration diagram.
